title: A dolphin named Bubbles makes other fish vomit, then eats it
gist: A male bottlenose dolphin nicknamed Bubbles at Australia's Lady Elliott Island Eco Resort has been documented chasing individual bigeye trevally until they vomit from stress, then eating the regurgitated food without eating the fish. A paper in Ecology and Evolution reports 20 foraging sightings between June 2021 and October 2025, 11 of them kleptoparasitic, and argues the behavior is a learned, low-energy foraging strategy that may be underreported in the wild.

insights.claim: A male bottlenose dolphin nicknamed Bubbles, present off the southern Great Barrier Reef since at least 2017, regularly chases local bigeye trevally until the stressed fish vomits what it has eaten, then devours the regurgitated food.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A specific, repeatable foraging tactic observed in the wild over years — the kind of durable behavioral record that supports a real scientific claim.
insights.locator: Bubbles has been around since at least 2017

insights.claim: Between June 2021 and October 2025 the authors collected 20 documented foraging sightings of Bubbles, of which 11 involved kleptoparasitic behavior.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Over half of observed foraging events used the tactic, suggesting it is a primary strategy rather than an occasional quirk.
insights.locator: the authors collected 20 documented foraging sightings

insights.claim: The foraging sequence is stereotyped: Bubbles scans with echolocation to select a target, chases that single fish while ignoring the rest of the school, mirrors its direction closely, and only breaks off when the fish vomits — repeating the cycle up to 10 times in half an hour.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The repeatable structure is what distinguishes a learned strategy from opportunistic scavenging.
insights.locator: First, Bubbles would scan the environment using echolocation

insights.claim: Bubbles only performs this behavior with bigeye trevally, and never eats the fish itself — only the regurgitated contents.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Species-specific targeting plus sparing the host points to deliberate strategy rather than failed predation.
insights.locator: he only seems to do this with bigeye trevally

insights.claim: Although dolphins usually forage in groups and Bubbles is occasionally seen with others, he prefers to forage alone when using this technique.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Solitary execution supports the idea of an individually invented rather than socially transmitted behavior.
insights.locator: While dolphins usually forage in groups

insights.claim: The technical term for this behavior is kleptoparasitism, usually involving one species taking food from another via aggressive confrontation, and it is widespread among bees and wasps, bears, coyotes, wolves, raptors, gulls, terns, bald eagles, skuas, frigatebirds, masked shrikes, Eurasian blackbirds, hyenas and jackals.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Food theft is a convergent strategy across the animal kingdom — the puzzle is why it is so rare in the water.

insights.claim: Kleptoparasitism is exceedingly rare among aquatic species, with the main marine-mammal precedent being reports of Risso's dolphins charging at sperm whales and consuming the regurgitated food.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Rarity in the marine environment is precisely what makes a single documented case scientifically valuable.
insights.locator: there have been reports of Risso’s dolphins charging at sperm whales

insights.claim: Co-author Asia Haines argues the behavior looks like learning: Bubbles developed a feeding strategy requiring less energy-intensive effort than chasing fast-swimming prey, and by repeating it over years 'may have learnt to target the fish with the fullest bellies, providing the most rewarding meals.'
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Energy-efficiency framing explains why an intelligent predator would prefer stolen half-digested food over live prey.
insights.quote: We observed him repeating this behavior over several years, which suggests he may have learnt to target the fish with the fullest bellies
insights.locator: This seems to be learned behavior, according to Haines

insights.claim: Haines pushes back on the popular image of dolphins as the 'good guys of the sea,' attributing it to anthropomorphism and the fact that dolphins appear to be smiling, and stressing that they are predators that actively hunt prey whether or not it was stolen.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A clean example of how a species' facial morphology distorts public and even scientific expectations of its behavior.
insights.quote: This perception of dolphins as the ‘good guys of the sea’ has more to do with anthropomorphism—our tendency to assign human characteristics to them
insights.locator: said co-author Asia Haines of the University of the Sunshine Coast

insights.claim: The authors hypothesize Bubbles identifies recently fed fish via echolocation during the scanning phase, noting other species use echolocation to distinguish fish species because different shapes return differently structured echoes.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: If confirmed, it would mean dolphins can acoustically read the contents of another animal's stomach — a notable sensory capability.
insights.locator: How can Bubbles even tell which fish have just eaten

insights.claim: The team sampled Bubbles' vocalizations from video footage and found an intense sequence of clicks and low-frequency tones during kleptoparasitism, but cannot tell whether these identify targets or deliberately increase the target's stress response.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The second interpretation would make the vocalizations a weapon rather than a sensor — a much stronger claim awaiting evidence.
insights.locator: The team did sample Bubbles’s vocalizations from the video footage

insights.claim: The study rests on a sample size of one animal (N=1) with a limited dataset, so more evidence from other dolphins in the region is needed before concluding the behavior is common in the species rather than unique to Bubbles.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: An explicitly stated N=1 limitation is the main reason to treat the generalization cautiously.
insights.locator: This is also a small sample size (N=1) and a limited dataset

insights.claim: The authors believe kleptoparasitic foraging may be substantially underestimated because it is so hard to capture on video in the wild, and predict that animal-borne video camera tags and drones will generate new insights into these cryptic behaviors.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Cheap sensor platforms are poised to expand observed behavioral repertoires in marine biology — an instrumentation-driven discovery wave.
insights.quote: The use of technologies such as animal-borne video camera tags and unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) are likely to generate new insights into the cryptic behaviors of these elusive marine predators
